opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting tradeoff, and I think people sometimes frame it too simplistically, either "probes are a silver bullet because we can read the model's mind" or "probes are useless because the model can just learn to evade them." The truth is somewhere in between, and it depends a lot on how you deploy them.

The big upside is cost and coverage. A linear probe on a model's activations is incredibly cheap. You're already computing those activations during the forward pass, so adding a probe is essentially free compared to running a separate classifier model over every input and output. That means you can monitor everything, not just a sample, and you get a signal that's grounded in the model's internal representations rather than just surface text. In principle that makes probes more robust to things like obfuscated prompts or jailbreaks that fool a text-based filter, because the model still has to internally represent that it's, say, helping with a bioweapons synthesis route.

The downside, and this is where a lot of our research has focused, is what happens under optimization pressure. If you train against a probe, use it as a loss term or in a reward signal, you're giving gradient descent a very direct incentive to reshape the representations so the probe stops firing, without necessarily changing the underlying behavior. We've seen that models can learn to obfuscate their activations surprisingly easily. Even without training against the probe, an adversary with white-box access, or even just clever input-space attacks, can often find inputs that push activations out of the region the probe was trained on. So you shouldn't think of a probe as reading some ground-truth "intent" feature. It's a classifier on a learned representation, and that representation can shift.

So how do I weigh it? A few principles. First, defense in depth. Probes are a great layer: cheap, broad, and with failure modes that are somewhat decorrelated from those of black-box input and output classifiers. Combining them makes an attacker's job much harder than either alone. Second, be very careful about training against your monitors. If a probe is your detection mechanism, keep it out of the training loop, or at least hold out some probes you never optimize against, so you have an uncorrupted signal. Third, think about the threat model. Against a casual misuser poking at an API, probes are probably quite effective. Against a sophisticated adversary with weight access, or a model that might itself be strategically trying to evade monitoring, you need to assume they can be beaten and treat them as one input to a broader system.

And finally, I'd say we need much more rigorous red-teaming of these safeguards before anyone relies on them for high-stakes decisions. The cheapness is genuinely exciting, but cheap and broken isn't a good deal. The question is always: what does it cost an attacker to get past this, relative to what it costs us to deploy it? On that metric probes look pretty good as part of a layered defense, and pretty risky as a standalone guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response says probe computation is essentially free because the main model’s activations are already computed during its forward pass.

r002.rationale: It says probes may catch obfuscated prompts that fool text-based filters, but does not identify a separate smaller language model as the comparison or say it might fail to understand them.

r003.rationale: The response describes probe failures as somewhat decorrelated from black-box classifiers; it does not explain that defenses relying on the same main-model activations have more correlated failures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that probes are one of the cheapest safeguards you can deploy, and that cheapness is both the appeal and the thing you have to be careful about.

The appeal is pretty straightforward. You've already got the activations sitting there from the forward pass. Training a linear probe on top of them costs almost nothing, and inference overhead is basically a dot product. Compare that to running a separate classifier model, or worse, a full second language model as a monitor, and you're talking orders of magnitude difference in compute. So if you're a lab serving billions of queries a day, probes are the kind of thing you can actually afford to run on every single request, whereas the more expensive monitors you can only sample. That coverage matters a lot. A safeguard that runs on one percent of traffic has a very different threat model than one that runs on all of it.

And there's a second thing people sometimes underrate, which is that probes read internal state rather than just the output text. So in principle they can catch things a text classifier would miss, like a model that's deliberately being evasive in its wording, or cases where the harmful intent is distributed across a conversation in a way that's hard to pick up from any single message.

Now, the tradeoffs. The big one is robustness. A linear probe is a very simple decision boundary in a very high dimensional space, and simple decision boundaries are easy to walk around. We've seen in our own work that if you can optimize against a probe, whether through adversarial suffixes or just through some fairly dumb iterative search, you can often find inputs that trigger the behavior you care about without lighting up the probe. The question then is whether the adversary actually has that kind of access. If the probe is behind an API and the attacker only gets a binary refused-or-not signal, that's a much harder optimization problem than if the probe weights leak. So I think of probe robustness as very much contingent on the deployment context, not as a fixed property.

The second tradeoff is distribution shift. Probes are trained on a dataset of what you think the bad behavior looks like, and they generalize in ways that are hard to predict. Sometimes they generalize surprisingly well, you train on one category of harm and they pick up related things. But sometimes they latch onto superficial features, like the tone of the request, or whether certain keywords appear, and then you get both false negatives on novel attacks and false positives on benign edge cases. And the false positives have real costs. If your safeguard is refusing legitimate security researchers or medical questions, you erode trust and people route around the system.

The third thing is that the probe is only as good as your understanding of what you're probing for. If you're looking for a concept the model represents cleanly, like whether it's being asked about a specific hazardous domain, great. If you're trying to probe for something fuzzier, like deception or scheming, you're making an assumption that there's a linearly readable direction for that, and the evidence there is a lot more mixed. I'd be nervous about anyone treating a deception probe as a strong guarantee right now.

So where does that leave me on the overall evaluation? I'd say probes are a good first layer, not a last line of defense. You want them in a defense-in-depth setup where they do the cheap filtering, and anything they flag, or some random sample of what they don't flag, gets escalated to more expensive and more robust monitoring. And critically, you want to be red teaming them continuously, because the failure mode I worry about most isn't that probes don't work, it's that they work well enough on your eval set that people stop looking.

The other thing I'd push on is that we should be investing in making them harder to evade, and there's actually decent progress there. Ensembling across layers, training against adversarial examples, probing for multiple correlated features rather than one. None of that makes them bulletproof, but it shifts the cost-benefit for an attacker. And given how cheap the baseline is, you can afford to spend a bit more and still be far below the cost of the alternatives.

r001.rationale: The response says probes reuse activations from the main model’s forward pass, making training and inference inexpensive.

r002.rationale: It says internal-state probes may catch evasive wording missed by a text classifier, but does not explain that the main model’s representations can reveal obfuscation a separate smaller language model might miss.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe correlated failures from defenses that rely on the same main-model activations.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is that you’re getting access to a much richer source of information, but you’re also putting more trust in your ability to interpret it. If you only look at a model’s outputs, you might miss something that’s detectable in its internal activations. A probe could give you an additional signal that the model is doing something concerning, even when its answer looks innocuous.

But a probe is itself a learned classifier. It might work well on the examples you trained and tested it on without detecting the thing you actually care about in a new setting. Maybe it’s picking up a correlate of deceptive behavior rather than deception itself. And if someone is actively trying to evade the safeguard, that distinction becomes especially important.

So I’d be excited to use probes as an additional layer of defense. I’d be much more cautious about treating a probe’s silence as strong evidence that a model is safe. The key question is how much additional protection it gives you under realistic attempts to circumvent it, and at what false-positive rate. That’s an empirical question, and I’d want the deployment decision to be grounded in those tests.

r001.rationale: The response discusses probes as an additional signal but does not mention reusing already computed activations or low deployment overhead.

r002.rationale: It says internal activations may reveal concerning behavior missed in outputs, but does not explain detecting obfuscation or compare probes with a separate smaller language model.

r003.rationale: It notes that a probe can fail to detect the target behavior and may be evaded, but does not identify correlated failures from defenses relying on the same main-model activations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key tradeoff is that activations potentially give you a much richer signal than the model’s outputs, but it’s harder to know exactly what that signal means and when you can trust it. A model might produce a perfectly innocuous answer while internally representing something concerning. If we can detect that, that’s a useful additional layer of defense.

But a probe that performs well on a held-out dataset isn’t necessarily a robust safeguard. It might be picking up on something correlated with the behavior you care about, and that correlation could break under distribution shift or when someone deliberately tries to evade it. So I’d want to evaluate the whole system under adaptive attack: can an adversary get the model to do the harmful thing while keeping the probe quiet?

There’s also a practical tradeoff around false positives. If you intervene whenever a model represents a dangerous concept, you may block legitimate work, including discussing how to prevent that danger. Representing something isn’t the same as intending to do it.

So I’m interested in probes as one component of a defense in depth. The question is how much additional security they buy you, at what cost to usefulness, and how well that improvement survives an adversary who knows the safeguard is there.
